articles.title: After 20 years, Seattle steam-cleaned about 2,350 pounds of gum from Pike Place Market in 2015 as the sticky landmark spread across its brick wall
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating history of Seattle's Gum Wall at Pike Place Market, its quirky origins, the massive clean-up in 2015, and how this colorful display continues to attract visitors.
articles.body: For years, visitors to Seattle’s Pike Place Market added their own small contribution to one of the city’s strangest landmarks: a wad of chewed gum pressed onto a brick wall. By 2015, however, the colourful attraction had become more than a quirky tourist tradition. After roughly two decades of accumulation, the gum had formed a thick layer that officials feared could damage the historic brickwork. The solution was as unusual as the attraction itself: workers brought in industrial steam cleaners and stripped away the entire collection.From theatre queue to tourist landmarkAccording to Pike Place Market, the Gum Wall began in the 1990s when local patrons and performers at Unexpected Productions started sticking used chewing gum onto the brick wall in Post Alley. The tradition began as a spontaneous habit among people waiting to enter the theatre, with some early visitors even pressing pennies into the gum. By the mid-1990s, the wall was already covered, and although attempts were made to remove the gum, visitors repeatedly rebuilt the display. Over time, what began as an informal act by theatre-goers developed into a colourful landmark, with thousands of pieces forming patterns, names and small artworks across the brick. Pike Place Market now describes the wall as a hidden work of art that continues to expand along Post Alley.The wall's persistence was helped by the physical properties of chewing gum. Unlike many food residues, chewing gum does not readily dissolve in water or disappear after it is discarded. The gum base is formulated to remain elastic and cohesive during chewing, allowing discarded pieces to retain their structure after they are pressed onto a surface. As successive visitors added more gum, the older pieces remained in place and became part of an increasingly thick layer. What began as a handful of pieces left by people waiting for a show eventually became a wall-sized accumulation that was difficult to remove without specialised cleaning.The great 2015 clean-upThe clean-up began in November 2015, turning an attraction that normally drew tourists into an unusual maintenance operation. Rather than scraping away the gum piece by piece, workers used an industrial steam machine to soften the accumulated mass so it could be removed from the brick. A small crew then collected the loosened gum in buckets. Pike Place Market later recorded that more than 2,000 pounds of gum were removed from Post Alley after roughly two decades of accumulation. Contemporary reports put the final amount at about 2,350 pounds, or more than a tonne of chewing gum.The sheer volume illustrated how dramatically the informal tradition had grown. Steam cleaning was used to loosen the gum without resorting to more aggressive methods that could damage the underlying masonry. This was particularly important because the wall forms part of the historic Pike Place Market area, where preserving older building materials is a consideration during maintenance and restoration work.Once the gum was removed, the brick wall looked almost unrecognisable. Yet the clean-up did not end the tradition. Visitors soon began sticking fresh pieces of gum back onto the exposed bricks, effectively restarting the landmark's strange cycle. The 2015 operation therefore became less a permanent end to the Gum Wall than a reset, removing decades of accumulated material while leaving the unusual tradition itself intact.The gum came backThe market had no intention of permanently ending the tradition. Officials treated the 2015 operation as a reset rather than a final closure. Once the accumulated gum had been removed, visitors were allowed to resume sticking fresh pieces onto the wall. Within days, the colourful coating was already beginning to return.TIME reported that a flash mob gathered at the newly cleaned wall, with visitors quickly adding fresh gum to the exposed brick. What had required industrial equipment and a major clean-up effort was recreated almost immediately by the public. The rapid return of the gum became part of the wall's identity, turning the 2015 removal into a temporary interruption rather than an end to the tradition.Pike Place Market has since continued to manage the attraction through periodic maintenance. Steam cleaning is used to remove accumulated gum from the surrounding Post Alley walls and help keep the display within its designated area. The Gum Wall itself, however, remains part of the visitor experience. Each new piece added to the bricks continues a tradition that began as a spontaneous habit outside a theatre and eventually became one of Seattle's most unusual landmarks.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: SHILLONG: The Meghalaya high court has quashed an FIR against six students from Uttar Pradesh accused of vandalising a homestay here after they paid Rs 2.06 lakh as compensation.Reportedly, officials said on Tuesday that two of the students were directed to pay an additional Rs 25,000 each and perform six days of community service.Chief Justice Revati Mohite Dere passed the order on Monday after the parties reached a mutual settlement, news agency PTI reported.The homestay manager and proprietor gave their no-objection to the quashing of the FIR, officials said.The FIR was registered at Laitumkhrah Police Station on July 11 following a complaint alleging that the homestay had been vandalised and that they left without paying.Police had also said the students smoked, consumed alcohol and brought outside visitors, allegedly violating house rules.A video showing the damaged rooms and bathroom of the recently opened property had subsequently surfaced on social media.The students were also accused of threatening the complainant after additional guests were not allowed to stay in a room beyond the permitted number, PTI reported.The accused subsequently approached the high court seeking quashing of the FIR.Three of them are minors, one aged 15 and two aged 17, while another had just turned 18.The remaining two students are in their 20s and preparing for competitive examinations, officials said.All six accused were arrested in West Bengal on July 13 following the incident and were subsequently released on bail.The parties entered into a mutual settlement on August 17 after elders and well-wishers of the students intervened, the court noted.Under the settlement, the students paid Rs 2.06 lakh to the homestay proprietor as full and final compensation.They also tendered a sincere and unconditional apology for their behaviour and actions, PTI reported.Justice Dere said there was no impediment to quashing the FIR, taking into Sabha in Lachumiere in Shillong from 10 am to 5 pm, under the supervision of Dr Kamaljeet Singh," an official said.They will also spend time with Jiva Cares' 'Project Operation Clean-Up', which articles.title: Shakespeare’s Globe needs a new roof after nearly 30 years, but workers will not use modern roofing; 14,000 bundles of reed are being prepared for the £10 million project
articles.summary: UK News: Shakespeare’s Globe in London is preparing for a major roof replacement nearly 30 years after the reconstructed theatre opened. The work will use trad.
articles.body: Shakespeare’s Globe in London is preparing for a major roof replacement nearly 30 years after the reconstructed theatre opened. The work will use traditional thatching methods rather than modern roofing materials, keeping the building’s historic character intact.The project will require about 14,000 bundles of reed for the new roof. The use of thatch is significant because Shakespeare’s Globe already has a thatched roof and has special permission to have one. According to the Globe, London has had a law against thatched buildings since the Great Fire of 1666.The reconstruction of the Globe was the idea of American actor Sam Wanamaker, rather than London’s mayor or the government. The theatre was built using traditional materials and methods, with more than 1,000 English oak trees measured during construction. About 600 oak trees were eventually used to build the Globe.The roof is therefore not simply a covering for the theatre. Thatch is part of how the reconstructed Globe was designed to reflect the appearance and construction of the original building. The replacement project will continue that approach, using reed instead of replacing the traditional roof with a modern material.Why reed matters to traditional thatchingReed is one of the traditional materials used for thatched buildings in England. Traditional thatching materials, skills and techniques are important for maintaining the local character of historic buildings and areas.The availability of good-quality cereal straw and water reed is a key part of maintaining traditional thatching. However, producing these materials has become more difficult over time.Before the middle of the 20th century, most thatching materials were sourced locally. Since the Second World War, materials and labour have become more mobile, while building techniques have also become more standardised. This has weakened some regional traditions.At the same time, the use of imported water reed from Eastern Europe and elsewhere increased. This was followed by a decline in UK production of water reed for thatch. The greater use of imported reed also reduced the market for thatching straw, as some thatchers considered imported water reed a more reliable alternative.These changes have created challenges for the traditional thatching industry. Producers now face issues including poor harvests, old machinery and uncertain seasonal labour supplies. Historic England says these pressures have left traditional thatching material production vulnerable.Preparing materials for traditional roofsThe Globe’s roof replacement comes as efforts are also being made to support the supply of traditional thatching materials in England.Historic England’s Traditional Thatch Project aims to support the production and use of good-quality indigenous thatching materials. The project is intended to create a more predictable and consistent supply and support the long-term sustainability of traditional thatching.As part of its work, Historic England has studied the problems faced by producers of thatching straw and water reed. It has also worked with growers and producers to understand what is already being done and what further steps could help increase the supply and resilience of these materials.The organisation has also looked at the machinery used to produce thatching straw. Unlike ordinary cereal straw, thatching straw cannot be harvested using a modern combine harvester.Some producers have tested changes to machinery and harvesting methods, but many still depend on traditional machines that are no longer produced. These machines can require significant maintenance, while finding spare parts can also be difficult.Improving harvesting and processing could make production safer, less labour-intensive and more financially viable. More efficient harvesting could also reduce the impact of adverse weather and ease pressure caused by labour shortages.A roof built around traditional methodsThe use of reed at Shakespeare’s Globe follows the theatre’s original approach to its reconstruction. When the Globe was built, about 6,000 bundles of reeds from Norfolk were used for its thatched roof. The theatre notes that Norfolk’s reed beds produce about 4,000 bundles a year, meaning the original roof required around a year and a half of reed supply.The building itself contains several other features based on traditional construction. Its walls were made using plaster containing goat hair, while the bricks in its foundations are copies of Tudor bricks.The Globe also has two large pillars on its stage, each made from a single oak tree. Builders had to measure many trees to find two that were the right size.The reconstructed theatre first hosted a performance in 1993, although the building was still under construction at the time. That first performance was in German.Today, Shakespeare’s Globe can hold about 1,500 people, around half the capacity of the original Globe. The theatre says this difference is partly because people today are bigger and modern audiences are less willing to stand closely packed together. Safety regulations have also changed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Maldives president seeks talks with UK PM on Chagos sovereignty
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Expressing concerns over the UK's decision to proceed with the handover of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, Maldivian president Mohamed Muizzu has wri.
articles.body: Expressing concerns over the UK's decision to proceed with the handover of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, Maldivian president Mohamed Muizzu has written to the British PM, Andrew Burnham, inviting him for official talks and engagement on matters concerning the sovereignty of the Chagos Islands.In the letter, Muizzu highlighted the shared history and cultural ties between the Maldives and Chagos, as well as the Maldives’ longstanding support for major marine conservation and scientific research expeditions in the region."In this regard, he reaffirmed the Maldives’ commitment to maintaining a reliable and constructive partnership with the United Kingdom on matters relating to Chagos, while safeguarding the legitimate interests of the Maldivian state and its people," said a statement issued by the president's office.Maldives’ position on Chagos is of interest to India as New Delhi has consistently supported Mauritius’s claim for sovereignty over Chagos, in line with its principled stand on decolonization and support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of nations, as well as its longstanding and close partnership with Mauritius.India has welcomed the agreement between the UK and Mauritius on the return of Mauritian sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago, including Diego Garcia, saying this significant understanding completed the decolonisation of Mauritius.Muizzu, however, reiterated the importance of meaningful dialogue between the UK and the Maldives on matters concerning the sovereignty of the Chagos Archipelago. "He further expressed hope that renewed engagement and partnership between the two countries would contribute to stability and security in the Indian Ocean, particularly at a time of increasing global uncertainty," said the Maldives' statement.According to a Maldivian spokesperson, Muizzu urged Burnham to address what he said was the previous British government’s failure to consult Malé over the proposed transfer, and to engage directly with the Maldives on its "longstanding concerns".The Chagos Islands are in the Indian Ocean approximately 280 nautical miles from Maldives and have been under British control since the early nineteenth century. In 2025, the British government agreed to transfer sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius, while retaining access to the joint UK-US military facility on Diego Garcia through a long-term lease, at an average cost of approximately £101 million per year.The Maldives opposes the proposed transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius and maintains a longstanding claim to the Chagos Archipelago, rooted in "historic ties, shared culture and geographic proximity to the islands".“A renewed partnership between Maldives and United Kingdom can bring stability to the Indian Ocean at a time of global uncertainty,” said Muizzu in his letter.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: After losing 90% of their ancestral territory during the Gold Rush, the Yurok Tribe has regained 125 acres as a gateway to California's redwoods
articles.summary: US News: After losing more than 90 per cent of their land during the upheaval of the mid-1800s, the Yurok Tribe has regained a 125-acre section of its ancestra.
articles.body: After losing more than 90 per cent of their land during the upheaval of the mid-1800s, the Yurok Tribe has regained a 125-acre section of its ancestral territory in Northern California. The land, known as ‘O Rew, was transferred back to the Yurok Tribe by Save the Redwoods League on 30 June 2026 after more than a decade of conservation and restoration work. According to Save the Redwoods League, the property is now tribally owned and operated, with the project also protecting critical salmon habitat. Once the site of a lumber mill where much of Prairie Creek’s natural channel and floodplain had been buried, ‘O Rew has been transformed into a restored landscape beside Redwood National and State Parks. The property now forms the ‘O Rew Redwoods Gateway, a public recreation area with new trails, wildlife habitat and exhibits presenting the Yurok perspective and language. Located off US Highway 101 near Orick, the gateway also provides access to some of the region’s old-growth coast redwood forests, including Lady Bird Johnson Grove. At the same time, plans include a cultural centre and a traditional village.Why is the Yurok Tribe getting 125 acres backSave the Redwoods League purchased and conserved ‘O Rew in 2013, initially intending to restore a severely degraded section of Prairie Creek while improving recreational access and connectivity. According to the National Park Service, the 2024 agreement was the first step towards transferring the 125-acre property to the Yurok Tribe and establishing a long-term co-stewardship arrangement. The agreement makes the site tribally owned and operated, permanently protecting critical salmon habitat and creating a new public space.The transfer followed years of planning and restoration involving the Yurok Tribe, Save the Redwoods League, California Trout and other agencies and partners. The National Park Service had described the 2024 agreement as a first step towards transferring ‘O Rew to the Yurok Tribe, with a shared vision for long-term co-stewardship of the property as a gateway to the neighbouring Redwood National and State Parks. The NPS said the arrangement would be the first in which it and California State Parks supported visitation and stewardship on Tribal-owned land.How did restoration transform the landscapeThe restoration changed a heavily altered landscape into a site with new wetlands, upland habitat and a redesigned Prairie Creek channel. Over five years, restoration crews built a one-mile braided channel, two off-channel ponds and 20 acres each of wetlands and upland habitat. The Yurok Revegetation Crew planted nearly half a million native seedlings representing 50 species, including coast redwoods and black cottonwood.The restored habitat is already being used by wildlife. Save the Redwoods League reported that hundreds of endangered juvenile coho salmon, western pond turtles and great blue herons were using habitat created during the project, while bears, elk, deer, condors, waterfowl, songbirds and other species had also returned to the site. Earlier National Park Service reporting said thousands of juvenile coho and Chinook salmon and steelhead were taking advantage of the restored habitat, alongside species including red-legged frogs, northwestern salamanders, elk and waterfowl.What can visitors experience at the ‘O Rew Redwoods GatewayThe ‘O Rew Redwoods Gateway opened for recreational access on 1 August 2026 at the southern end of Redwood National and State Parks. The site includes an information kiosk designed to resemble a traditional Yurok house, along with interpretive exhibits using Yurok perspectives and language. It also has a pedestrian plaza, picnic tables, accessible trails and an elevated viewpoint over the restored landscape and surrounding forest.The new trails include a segment of the California Coastal Trail and connect with Redwood National and State Parks, providing access towards old-growth coast redwood stands including Lady Bird Johnson Grove. The Yurok Tribe also plans to construct a cultural centre and a traditional village on the property, with plank houses and a sweat house. The National Park Service said the planned gateway would highlight local Tribal histories and cultures, while the Yurok Tribe’s return to the property forms part of a wider effort to reclaim and restore culturally important landscapes across its ancestral territory.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2024, Wales used fibres recovered from about 80,000 used nappies to resurface a road, diverting four tonnes of waste from landfill at no extra material cost
articles.summary: UK News: What if the disposable diaper changed a baby’s day, and then went on to help build the road outside your home? An unusual recycling experiment in Wale.
articles.body: What if the disposable diaper changed a baby’s day, and then went on to help build the road outside your home? An unusual recycling experiment in Wales has transformed thousands of used diapers into an unexpected ingredient for road construction, offering a glimpse into how everyday waste could become a valuable resource. Carmarthenshire County Council’s official website says that in the past, they teamed up with local recycling company Nappicycle on a trial project aimed at solving two problems at once: the growing amount of nappy waste and the effect of traditional road maintenance on the environment. The first trial, on the B4336 at Pontweli in March 2024, took around four tons of used diapers—the equivalent of some 80,000 diapers—out of landfill. The project was particularly significant considering that, in 2023 alone, Carmarthenshire collected around 6 million diapers, underlining the size of the waste stream and the opportunity to seek new applications for it.How road material is made from used diapersAccording to the report, the process started with the council collecting the waste diapers. The materials were then taken to Nappicycle's recycling facility in Capel Hendre where they were processed and turned into fibrous pellets. The recycled fibers were then taken to the contractor GD Harries’ plant in Ludchurch. Before being laid onto the road, they were mixed with a road-surfacing material, called Stone Mastic Asphalt (SMA). The council said that the recycled nappy fibers were as effective as conventional materials and the trial cost had no additional material.A local circular economyThe project is a brilliant example of the circular economy in action; used diapers are not treated as waste to be sent to landfill, but are instead recovered for their materials and given a new lease of life. The approach could help cut waste and promote more sustainable highway maintenance by using recycled material in place of some virgin resources. Reducing the carbon footprint of waste disposal may also be a benefit of keeping diapers out of landfill. And since the recycling and subsequent manufacturing is done locally, the initiative can also reduce the transportation and processing that comes with sourcing and disposing of materials.Could diapers shape the future?For Carmarthenshire the road trial is but a beginning. If successful, the council says it will consider expanding the initiative, potentially turning an everyday waste problem into a long-term infrastructure solution. Cabinet Member for Climate Change, Decarbonization and Sustainability, Councilor Aled Vaughan Owen, said the project was an example of responsibility and innovation when it came to the environment, showing how used diapers can have a useful second life rather than being dumped in landfill.Images Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India rolls out 400th Apache fuselage as defence sector takes off
articles.summary: News News: Tata Boeing Aerospace Limited has rolled out the 400th fuselage for the AH-64E Apache, one of the world’s most advanced attack helicopters, from its f.
articles.body: Tata Boeing Aerospace Limited has rolled out the 400th fuselage for the AH-64E Apache, one of the world’s most advanced attack helicopters, from its facility in India.The joint venture between Boeing and Tata Advanced Systems Limited manufactures the fuselages domestically, which are then integrated into the final aircraft supplied to customers worldwide, including the US Army.India has also received six Apaches for the Indian Army, while the Indian Air Force operates a fleet of 22 AH-64E helicopters.With roughly 1,300 Apaches currently in service across 19 countries, the milestone highlights the scale of India’s role in the programme: nearly 30% of all Apaches ever built have had their fuselages manufactured in India.The achievement is also part of a much larger transformation in India’s defence manufacturing sector.According to figures provided by the Defence Ministry, indigenous defence production rose from Rs 46,429 crore in 2014-15 to Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26. Production increased 15.6% over the previous year alone and has more than doubled since FY 2020-21.Defence exports have grown even more sharply. From just Rs 686 crore in 2013-14, exports reached a record Rs 38,424 crore in 2025-26. Indian defence products are now being exported to more than 80 countries, with over 145 companies actively engaged in exports.The government has set a target of Rs 50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029, a goal officials believe is achievable given the sector’s current trajectory.Supporting this expansion is a rapidly broadening defence industrial base comprising 16 Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs), around 500 licensed defence manufacturers and nearly 17,000 MSMEs directly involved in defence production. The industry is also becoming more geographically diverse, with defence manufacturing spreading beyond traditional hubs and gaining momentum through the defence industrial corridors in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.The sector has attracted investment commitments of nearly Rs 75,000 crore, of which around Rs 10,800 crore has already translated into actual investment.The public sector has also shown signs of a significant turnaround. Recent reviews indicate that all 16 DPSUs are now operating profitably, while spending on research and development has increased and companies are increasingly pursuing opportunities in overseas markets.The shift marks a significant departure from an era when India’s defence industry was widely seen as slow-moving and the armed forces heavily dependent on imports. Today, the country is steadily positioning itself as a global defence manufacturing and supply hub.

articles.body: As the world grapples with mounting waste and rising carbon emissions, a bridge project in New York is offering an unusual example of how something destined for a landfill can be given a second life. In June 2024, construction began on a $21.2 million project in the Village of Whitney Point, where New York is replacing an ageing bridge over the Tioughnioga River and incorporating recycled glass into concrete used for parts of the new infrastructure. The pilot project is expected to divert 106 tons of waste glass from local landfills and prevent more than 72 tons of carbon dioxide emissions.The project is part of a broader push towards a circular economy, in which materials traditionally treated as waste are recovered and reused rather than discarded.Turning waste glass into a cement alternativeThe idea behind the project comes from KLAW Industries, a New York-based company founded in 2019 by Binghamton University engineering students Jacob Kumpon and Jack Lamuraglia. The founders saw two problems that could potentially be addressed together: the enormous amount of glass entering the US waste stream and the carbon-intensive nature of cement production.The US produces an estimated 12 million tons of glass every year. Of that, only about 3 million tons are recycled, leaving roughly 9 million tons of waste glass going to landfills annually. KLAW developed a technology that turns post-consumer glass into a fine powder that can partially replace conventional cement in concrete. The resulting material, called Pantheon, is designed to reduce the amount of cement required while maintaining or improving the concrete's strength.Rather than simply grinding glass and mixing it into concrete, KLAW's patented process removes unwanted materials from waste glass before producing Pantheon. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency, the resulting material reacts with cement and creates additional crystal structures within the concrete, helping strengthen it. The approach tackles two waste problems at once. It gives discarded glass another use while reducing the quantity of cement needed in concrete.From a college idea to a state infrastructure projectKumpon and Lamuraglia began developing the technology after recognising the potential of combining recycled materials with lower-carbon construction. KLAW later received support through the EPA's Small Business Innovation Research programme. Its first Phase I award was $100,000 and was used to establish proof of concept for a project titled “Prototyping a Process to Reuse Wasted Glass in High Performance Low Carbon Concrete.”The company worked with Binghamton-based concrete producer Barney & Dickenson to test and demonstrate the technology. Following the initial research, KLAW received a Phase II award to further test and promote its cement alternative.The technology subsequently attracted attention in Binghamton, where Pantheon was adopted for municipal projects. After several successful local applications, KLAW was approached by the New York State Department of Transportation for a much larger project in Whitney Point.The U.S. Route 11 bridge project became a significant milestone for the company. According to the EPA, it is KLAW's largest single-location project and its first state-sponsored project.A 77-year-old bridge gets a greener replacementThe project is replacing the existing U.S. Route 11 bridge over the Tioughnioga River, a three-span steel structure built in 1947. The bridge has been an important transportation link for the community, connecting people to businesses, recreational areas and community facilities. The route also provides access to Interstate 81 and state routes 26, 79 and 206. More than 11,000 vehicles travel through the project area on an average day.But the old structure was nearing the end of its service life and was also on New York State's High-Risk Flood Watch List. That designation meant it required round-the-clock monitoring whenever water levels reached a predetermined elevation.The replacement will use a multi-girder design intended to be less vulnerable to flooding. Once completed, the new structure is expected to be removed from the state's High-Risk Flood Watch List.The $21.2 million project includes more than the bridge. It also includes 1.5 miles of new ADA-compliant sidewalks along both sides of U.S. Route 11, stretching from Main Street to Keibel Road. New crosswalks are also being installed near Whitney Point Middle School and the Broome County Fairgrounds. Pantheon is being incorporated into concrete used for sidewalks, curbs and barriers on the new bridge, as well as the new sidewalks along U.S. Route 11.Why recycled glass mattersThe construction industry is one of the biggest opportunities for reducing the environmental impact of materials. Cement, a key ingredient in concrete, is particularly carbon-intensive.By allowing concrete producers to use less cement, Pantheon can reduce emissions without adding additional cost, according to the EPA. At the same time, the process creates a market for post-consumer glass that might otherwise be buried in landfills.The Whitney Point project also comes as New York moves to implement its Buy Clean Concrete Guidelines, announced in 2023, which encourage lower-carbon concrete and consideration of emissions associated with construction materials.For KLAW, the project represents more than an experiment with recycled materials. Company COO Jacob Kumpon described it as a turning point that marked the business's transition out of its startup phase. For New York, it is an opportunity to test whether waste-derived materials can become part of everyday public infrastructure.From landfill waste to public infrastructureThe significance of the project lies in its simplicity: glass that could have remained waste is being transformed into a material that becomes part of a bridge, sidewalks and other infrastructure.The 106 tons of glass diverted by the project may be modest compared with the millions of tons discarded across the US each year. But the pilot demonstrates how a material considered waste can be brought back into the production cycle.The new bridge is also being designed with resilience in mind, combining infrastructure upgrades with an attempt to lower the environmental footprint of construction. Work is expected to continue through late 2026. During construction, a temporary bridge has been built alongside the existing structure to accommodate pedestrians, bicycles and two-way vehicle traffic.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
